sections.title: Parent callback input
sections.what: Accepts one callback from the parent, used to move the user into the main desk after the intro.
sections.why: Likely reason: the intro does not decide where the user goes next; the parent does.

sections.name: CatKeyboardIntro (part 1)
sections.title: Screen state and fit to window
sections.what: Sets up the cat's initials, the scale that fits a 1200 by 800 design to the window, the speech bubble, the monitor text, the cat's position and the task input. The scale is also written to a global window value.
sections.why: Likely reason: the whole intro is designed for one fixed layout and scaled to fit smaller windows.
sections.watch_out: The scale is copied to a global window property, which other code could read or rely on without being told.

sections.name: CatKeyboardIntro: if
sections.title: Speech bubbles and wiggle reactions
sections.what: Shows a speech bubble for a set time and makes the cat wiggle. When someone types on the keyboard it picks a complaint from a short list in turn, such as the keyboard is warm.
sections.why: Likely reason: gives the cat a personality and explains why it blocks typing.
sections.watch_out: Bubble timers are replaced when a new message appears, but they are not cleared when the screen closes, so one may fire after the screen is gone.

sections.name: CatKeyboardIntro (part 3)
sections.title: Dragging the cat
sections.what: Lets the user drag the cat. If it is dragged more than 140 pixels it moves to a bed spot; if released sooner it jumps back to the keyboard with a remark.
sections.why: Likely reason: dragging is the main way to get the cat off the keyboard.
sections.watch_out: A movement of less than 6 pixels counts as a click rather than a drag, so tiny drags are treated as clicks.

sections.name: CatKeyboardIntro: if
sections.title: Clicks, typing and the paper form
sections.what: Clicking the cat counts as a nudge, and the second nudge sends it to bed. While the cat is on the keyboard, letters typed outside text boxes show fake keys and sometimes a complaint. Once the cat is gone, submitting the paper form adds the typed text as a high priority task for today in the Career category with a 30 minute estimate.
sections.why: Likely reason: the typing effect makes the screen feel responsive, and the paper form turns the morning setup into real tasks.
sections.watch_out: Every task added from the paper form is hard-coded to the Career category and 30 minutes, whatever the user intended.

sections.name: CatKeyboardIntro (part 5)
sections.title: Leaving the intro and key positions
sections.what: Leaves the intro after a half second fade by calling the parent callback. It also works out the positions of the keyboard keys using fixed sizes, and reads the first three tasks for the paper list.
sections.why: Likely reason: the key positions are worked out once so the drawing does not recalculate on every change.
sections.watch_out: The key layout depends on fixed pixel numbers, so changing the artwork means changing those numbers too.

sections.name: CatKeyboardIntro (part 6)
sections.title: Screen frame and text styles
sections.what: Starts the screen layout and defines the styles for the intro text, the monitor message, the typed text and the brand badge.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the hand-drawn look in one place.
sections.watch_out: The styles name specific fonts (Gaegu and VT323); if those fonts fail to load, the look changes.

sections.name: CatKeyboardIntro (part 7)
sections.title: Go button and cat styles
sections.what: Styles the go button, the cat's size and position, its drag, settle and wiggle animations, and the floating Z letters.
sections.why: Likely reason: shows the cat is draggable and gives visual cues for its states.
sections.watch_out: The cat's starting position is repeated in the code and in these styles, so both must change together.

sections.name: CatKeyboardIntro (part 8)
sections.title: Speech bubble and paper styles
sections.what: Styles the speech bubble and its pointer, the sheet of paper for the task list and its heading.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: CatKeyboardIntro (part 9)
sections.title: Paper form and skip button styles
sections.what: Styles the paper task list, its checkboxes, the input line, the add button including its disabled look, and the skip button at the bottom left.
sections.why: Likely reason: makes the paper look like a hand-written list.

sections.name: CatKeyboardIntro (part 10)
sections.title: Keyboard click area and screen start
sections.what: Finishes the skip button style, sets a transparent clickable area over the keyboard picture, and starts the intro markup with an accessible region label.
sections.why: Likely reason: the keyboard picture needs a clickable target placed over it.

sections.name: CatKeyboardIntro (part 11)
sections.title: Intro picture drawing
sections.what: Draws the picture: a cream wall, a blue floor, a monitor with a yellow note window, folder icons, sticker labels reading TO DO, the year and the user's initials, and a pencil cup.
sections.why: Likely reason: drawing the picture in code keeps it sharp at any size.
sections.watch_out: The year and initials are written onto the picture, so unusually long text could overflow its sticker.

summary: A playful opening screen where a cat sleeps on a drawn keyboard. The user drags or clicks the cat off, then writes today's tasks on a paper note, and then the desk opens.
purpose: Makes the morning setup feel like a short game and collects the first tasks for the day.
why: Likely reason: a friendly daily ritual that gets the user to plan before working.
how: The screen scales to fit the window and draws a monitor, keyboard and paper. Dragging the cat far enough moves it to a bed; two clicks also move it. Typing outside text boxes shows fake keys and cat complaints. Once the cat is gone, the paper form accepts text and adds a task. The screen then calls the parent's callback to enter the desk.
inputs: The current user and profile from the stores, the addTask action, the onEnterDesk callback, and mouse, pointer and keyboard events.
outputs: A new task added to the store with status today, high priority, the Career category and a 30 minute estimate. A call to onEnterDesk when the intro ends.
risks: Several fixed pixel positions are repeated in code and styles, so a layout change must touch both. Timers are not cleared when the screen closes. The keyboard listener on the whole window blocks typing outside text boxes while the cat is on the keyboard. The category and estimate are hard-coded. Sections 14 to 17 (lines 620 to 803) were not in the packet.
debug: If the cat will not move, check the drag threshold and pointer handlers. If the task is not added, confirm the cat has left and the input is not empty. If the intro never closes, check where leaveIntro is called; the reviewed code defines it but does not call it, so the caller is probably in the unreviewed part (not confirmed).
